issues.legal_issue: A challenge to an ordinance becomes infructuous when the ordinance has been replaced by legislation and no action taken under the ordinance remains for adjudication.
material_facts: A writ petition challenged an ordinance that was later replaced by an Act of Parliament.
The grounds challenging the ordinance were also raised in a separate petition challenging the Act.
No action taken under the ordinance remained whose legality required adjudication after the ordinance ceased to operate.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the ordinance was disposed of as infructuous without adjudication on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: When a challenged ordinance has ceased to operate after replacement by an Act, and no action taken under the ordinance remains to be adjudicated, the challenge to the ordinance is infructuous; the merits can be considered in a challenge to the replacement Act.

predicates.ordinance_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of an ordinance.
predicates.ordinance_replaced_by_legislation: The ordinance ceased to operate after being replaced by legislation.
predicates.no_surviving_action_under_ordinance: No action taken under the ordinance remains whose legality requires adjudication.

issues.definition: When an ordinance-validity challenge concerns an ordinance replaced by legislation and no action under it survives for adjudication, the challenge is disposed of as infructuous without a merits decision.

issues.legal_issue: Alleged political motives do not invalidate legislation when the enacting legislature has competence over its subject matter.
material_facts: The petitioners alleged that the legislation and the preceding ordinances were politically motivated.
The petitioners provided no particulars of the alleged political malice.
The Court examined Parliament's competence to enact the legislation.
issues.conclusion: The allegation of political malice did not provide a basis for invalidating the Act; the controlling question was legislative competence.
issues.legal_principle: Under K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa and Board of Trustees, Ayurvedic and Unani Tibia College v. State of Delhi, the doctrine of colourable legislation concerns legislative competence, not legislative bona fides or motives. If the legislature is competent, its motives are irrelevant; if it is not competent, motive is immaterial.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of legislation.
predicates.legislative_motive_alleged: A challenger alleges that the legislature acted from an improper or political motive.
predicates.legislature_has_subject_matter_competenc: The legislature has constitutional competence over the subject matter of the legislation.

issues.definition: If an improper legislative motive is alleged in a constitutional challenge but the enacting legislature has competence over the subject matter, the allegation does not invalidate the legislation.

issues.legal_issue: Taking over an institution and its activities does not violate citizens' freedom of speech or association when the voluntary association itself, its membership, and its governing body remain untouched.
material_facts: A registered society had established and operated an institution devoted to the study of world affairs.
The legislation declared the institution to be of national importance and transferred its activities, assets, and management to a new statutory body.
The society itself continued to exist, with its membership and governing body unchanged, and remained free to carry on other activities.
The petitioners claimed that the transfer violated freedom of speech and association.
issues.conclusion: The Act did not violate the rights to freedom of speech and expression or to form associations under Article 19(1)(a) and (c).
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(c) protects the right to form an association, not a fundamental right to achieve every object of the association or to control every activity or institution through which it operates. Restrictions on the association's activities are assessed under the relevant right governing those activities, not by expanding Article 19(1)(c). The rights of an association under Article 19 are those of its citizen members and cannot exceed their rights. The Court relied on State of Madras v. V.G. Row, All India Bank Employees' Association v. National Industrial Tribunal, Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, Tata Engineering and Locomotive Co. v. State, Azeez Basha v. Union of India, D.A.V. College v. State of Punjab, L.N. Mishra Institute v. State of Bihar, S.P. Mittal v. Union of India, and distinguished Damyanti Naranga v. Union of India and Asom Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti v. State of Assam. It also applied Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(c), 19(2), and 19(4).

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_legislation and association_right_claimed and association_remains_intact and (membership_unchanged and governing_body_unchanged)

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_legislation: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of legislation affecting an institution associated with a voluntary society.
predicates.association_right_claimed: The challengers claim that the legislation infringes citizens' rights of speech or association.
predicates.association_remains_intact: The voluntary association continues to exist after the legislation.
predicates.membership_unchanged: The legislation does not remove existing members or compel the association to accept new members.
predicates.governing_body_unchanged: The legislation does not alter the association's governing body.

issues.definition: When legislation is constitutionally challenged on speech or association grounds but leaves the voluntary association, its membership, and its governing body intact, those rights are not infringed merely because the association loses control of an institution or activity.

issues.legal_issue: A property-right challenge under Article 300A is not fit for determination in a writ proceeding when it is not properly pleaded and depends on disputed title facts that require evidence.
material_facts: The petitioners claimed that property belonging to the society had been taken over.
The Government disputed the petitioners' title to the land, building, and other claimed property.
The petitioners produced no title documents, and the title dispute could not be resolved without evidence.
The Court also noted that the Article 300A claim had not been made out in the writ petition and expressed doubt that the right could be enforced through an Article 32 petition.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to adjudicate the Article 300A challenge in the writ proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Article 300A protects persons, including legal persons, from deprivation of property except by authority of law. The Court considered the principles in Board of Trustees, Ayurvedic and Unani Tibia College v. State of Delhi, but held that a claim turning on unpleaded and highly disputed title facts requiring evidence was not suitable for determination in the writ proceeding; it also expressed grave doubt that the property right could be enforced by an Article 32 petition after the Forty-Fourth Amendment.

rule.if: article_300a_writ_challenge and property_title_disputed and title_requires_evidence and claim_not_properly_pleaded

predicates.article_300a_writ_challenge: The proceeding invokes a constitutional protection against deprivation of property and seeks relief by writ.
predicates.property_title_disputed: The government disputes the claimant's title to the property said to have been taken.
predicates.title_requires_evidence: Resolving the title dispute requires evidence rather than determination on the writ record.
predicates.claim_not_properly_pleaded: The property-right claim was not properly set out in the pleading.

issues.definition: When a writ-based property-right claim is inadequately pleaded and depends on disputed title requiring evidence, the court does not adjudicate that claim in the writ proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: Legislation addressing a single institution does not violate equality when the institution is an intelligible class and the classification bears a rational relation to the legislative object.
material_facts: Parliament enacted legislation concerning one institution declared to be of national importance.
Parliamentary committees had identified complaints and findings of mismanagement and maladministration at that institution.
The petitioners did not identify another institution shown to be comparable to it.
The legislation was directed at governing the institution and addressing the circumstances identified concerning it.
issues.conclusion: The Act was not arbitrary or unreasonable and did not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits class legislation but permits reasonable classification based on an intelligible differentia rationally related to the legislative object; the classification need not be scientifically perfect or logically complete. A single institution may constitute a class by itself when special circumstances justify legislation directed to it. The Court relied on S.P. Mittal v. Union of India, Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar, Raja Birakishore v. State of Orissa, Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India, Charanjit Lal Chowdhury v. Union of India, Board of Trustees, Ayurvedic and Unani Tibia College v. State of Delhi, and the principle that the availability of alternative legal remedies does not by itself invalidate legislation.

predicates.article_14_challenge_to_legislation: The proceeding challenges legislation as discriminatory or arbitrary under the constitutional equality guarantee.
predicates.institution_singled_out: The legislation applies to one institution rather than a general class of institutions.
predicates.institution_has_distinguishing_circumsta: The institution has circumstances distinguishing it from institutions not covered by the legislation.
predicates.distinguishing_circumstances_relational_: The circumstances distinguishing the institution bear a rational relation to the object of the legislation.

issues.definition: When legislation singles out an institution whose distinguishing circumstances rationally relate to the legislative object, the single-institution classification is not arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: A later enactment is not invalid merely because it contains provisions similar to those in an earlier ordinance that was struck down in a judgment that was not reviewed on appeal on its merits.
material_facts: A High Court single judge had struck down an earlier ordinance containing provisions similar to those later enacted.
The government appealed, but the appeal was dismissed as infructuous after the ordinance lapsed and the appellate court did not decide the merits.
Parliament later enacted the challenged legislation.
The Supreme Court independently examined the later Act and concluded that it was within Parliament's competence and constitutionally valid.
The Supreme Court found the earlier single-judge decision erroneous and expressly overruled it.
issues.conclusion: The Act was not invalid under the doctrine of separation of powers because of the earlier judgment; the earlier judgment was expressly overruled.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature may change the factual or legal basis on which a judicial decision proceeded, subject to legislative competence and constitutional limitations, but it cannot declare a court judgment void or exercise a judicial function. A later law must be examined for competence, compliance with constitutional requirements, and consistency with fundamental rights. The Court relied on Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills v. Broach Borough Municipality, Misrilal Jain v. State of Orissa, Madan Mohan Pathak v. Union of India, Union of India v. Raghubir Singh, Indian Aluminium Co. v. State of Kerala, Welfare Association A.R.P. v. Ranjit P. Gohil, People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India, and Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain. It held that the prior appellate proceeding left the matter open because it had ended without a merits decision and that the earlier ruling was erroneous.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_later_legisl: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of legislation enacted after an earlier ordinance.
predicates.earlier_ruling_concerned_expired_ordinan: An earlier court ruling invalidated an ordinance that later ceased to operate.
predicates.appeal_ended_without_merits: An appeal from the earlier ruling ended without appellate adjudication of its merits.
predicates.later_legislation_independently_reviewed: The court independently reviews the later legislation for constitutional validity and legislative competence.

issues.definition: When a later enactment is independently reviewed and the earlier ruling concerning an expired ordinance was not decided on appeal on its merits, that earlier ruling does not by itself invalidate the later enactment.

issues.legal_issue: Parliament may legislate for the management and administration of an institution declared by law to be of national importance within the relevant Union legislative fields.
material_facts: The Act declared the institution to be one of national importance.
The institution had received financial assistance from the Government of India at an earlier time.
The Act incorporated a statutory body and transferred the institution's activities, assets, and management to it.
The petitioners did not show that the Act's provisions encroached on a legislative field unavailable to Parliament.
issues.conclusion: The Act fell within Parliament's legislative competence under Entries 62 and 63 of List I of the Seventh Schedule.
issues.legal_principle: Entries 62 and 63 of List I permit Parliament to legislate concerning specified institutions and other institutions declared by law to be of national importance. Legislative entries are construed broadly to include the main subject and matters incidental or ancillary to it. The Court relied on British Coal Corporation v. The King, United Provinces v. Atiqa Begum, Navinchandra Mafatlal v. Commissioner of Income Tax, and Sri Ram Ram Narain Medhi v. State of Bombay.

rule.if: legislative_competence_challenge and institution_declared_of_national_importance and legislation_governs_institution and no_unavailable_field_encroached

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge: The proceeding challenges whether the national legislature had competence to enact legislation concerning an institution.
predicates.institution_declared_of_national_importa: The institution has been declared by law to be of national importance.
predicates.legislation_governs_institution: The legislation provides for the institution's incorporation, management, administration, or affairs.
predicates.no_unavailable_field_encroached: The challenger has not established that the legislation encroaches on a legislative field unavailable to the national legislature.

issues.definition: When an institution is declared to be of national importance and legislation governs its affairs without encroaching on an unavailable legislative field, Parliament has competence to enact that legislation.
